builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Tool-Calling LLM Agents Under Realistic MCP Faults: Scale Does Not Purchase Fault Tolerance
summary: MCP-Injector replaces clean-tool agent benchmarks (which assume correct, timely tool responses) with seedable, protocol-aware fault injection on the MCP call path, calibrated to failure modes mined from 57,240 real MCP repository threads. It costs an extra middleware layer in the tool-call path plus evaluation runtime; no model retraining or large hardware is required, so it fits a single-GPU or API-based setup. It can fail to predict production behavior if the mined incident distribution diverges from the reader's actual tool ecosystem, and results on gpt-oss backbones may not transfer to other model families.
rationale: The finding that framework-level error handling matters more than model scale is directly actionable for a constrained-infrastructure team: before adopting, they should validate the fault-injection harness against their own tool stack, since resilience claims depend on the agent framework and fault profile rather than on model size.
technique: Protocol-aware fault injection for MCP tool-call evaluation

claims.statement: MCP-Injector replaces clean-tool agent benchmarks (which assume correct, timely tool responses) with seedable, protocol-aware fault injection on the MCP call path, calibrated to failure modes mined from 57,240 real MCP repository threads. It costs an extra middleware layer in the tool-call path plus evaluation runtime; no model retraining or large hardware is required, so it fits a single-GPU or API-based setup. It can fail to predict production behavior if the mined incident distribution diverges from the reader's actual tool ecosystem, and results on gpt-oss backbones may not transfer to other model families.

Under a permanent-heavy fault profile, task-completion score falls 60% (8.08 to 3.23 of 10); the 120B backbone retains no larger share of its fault-free score than the 20B (p = 0.96), with completion under faults 91.1% vs 95.6% (95% CI [-0.2, 9.3] points).
